article.overview: A dust charging sensor is an instrument that measures the electrical charge carried by dust grains and, in some designs, also their size, velocity or arrival rate. On the Moon, ultraviolet light, X-rays and plasma can charge dust grains, and electrostatic forces may lift fine grains off the surface [3]. The catalogue name describes a measurement function rather than one standard device. The most fully documented example is the Electrostatic Dust Analyzer (EDA), which the authors describe as a flight-qualified prototype at technology readiness level 6, with no flight reported in the sources accessed [1]. Other charge-sensing or levitation-detection concepts are at breadboard, validation or design stage [3][6]. The only flown example in the sources accessed is the Apollo 17 Lunar Ejecta and Meteorites (LEAM) experiment, whose data were interpreted as dominated by electrostatically charged lunar fines rather than the hypervelocity impacts it was designed to detect [4][5]. Scope of this article. The article covers in-situ instruments and concepts that measure charge on lunar dust grains, and the observations needed to interpret that charge. It does not cover dust mitigation hardware, remote dust imaging or sample-return analysis. Cross-references to other catalogue entries, not duplicated here: 133 (Electrostatic dust analyser), the closest catalogue name match for the EDA example; 123 (Dust detector) and 124 (Micrometeoroid detector), which measure dust impacts rather than charge; 135 (Dust levitation experiment), which is closely related to the levitation concept discussed; and 119 (Langmuir probe) and 137 (Surface electric field detector), which measure the plasma and electric field that control dust charging.
article.description: A dust charging sensor measures how much electrical charge dust grains carry. Charge matters because electrostatic forces can lift fine dust off a surface, and charged dust can adhere to equipment and interact electrostatically with rover wheels, astronaut boots and other surfaces [2]. Charge alone does not give a grain's size or mass, so designs often add a velocity measurement and a deflection measurement. In the EDA, charge is derived from signals induced on wire electrodes, velocity from timing differences between wire arrays, and mass from the bending of each grain's trajectory in an electric field [1]. Other concepts use a charge-collecting probe with a Faraday-cup current measurement [6], or optical detection of levitated grains [3]. Instruments of this kind differ from impact detectors, which infer grain properties from the signal produced when a grain strikes a target.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a lunar dust charging sensor is to measure dust charge directly in situ, so that scientists can test whether electrostatic lofting moves dust and, if so, how much. The EDA paper states that there are no unambiguous in-space measurements confirming electrostatic dust lofting on the Moon, and that the EDA is intended to supply that ground truth [1]. Its stated measurement targets are the charge, velocity, size and flux of lofted grains [1]. The authors also state that its data could help assess crew safety and exploration-system risks, and inform surface evolution on airless bodies [1]. For surface operations, the same charging is a hazard, since regolith dust builds up charge and interacts electrostatically with equipment [2]. A sensor that measures that charge therefore serves both science and engineering needs.
article.operating_principle: Charge induction and trajectory reconstruction (EDA). A charged grain passing through the EDA's wire arrays induces a signal on each wire. The summed induced charge gives the grain's charge, and ratios of signals across the wires locate the grain and allow its velocity in the measurement plane to be reconstructed [1]. Each dust trajectory sensor has two arrays of seven wire electrodes, and each wire has its own charge-sensitive amplifier [1]. The grain then passes through a deflection field electrode with two positively biased plates and one negatively biased plate, and the deflection of its path gives its mass [1]. Size is derived by assuming a density of about 2.9 g cm-3 for the JSC-1A simulant or about 3 g cm-3 for typical lunar dust [1]. Electron-rejection grids at the entrances are biased between 0 and -125 V [1]. Other principles. The DUSTER dust probe is biased between -5000 V and +5000 V to attract dust, and the current from charged particles is measured in a Faraday cup [6]. The DLR concept uses a 532 nm pulsed laser and a stereo camera system to detect levitated grains [3]. The NASA multi-sensor concept measures charge from dust contact with space-rated materials, together with the electric-field distribution and ion currents near the surface [2].
article.scientific_importance: Charged lunar dust is a plausible explanation for observations that remain incompletely understood. Surveyor 6 observed a horizon glow at the terminator, which is now associated with dust levitation [3]. The Apollo 17 LEAM data were interpreted as dominated by electrostatically charged lunar fines, and the authors linked the events to terminator passages [4][5]. A direct measurement of charge, velocity and size would test whether electrostatic lofting actually supplies fine dust to the near-surface environment [1][3]. The scientific value of such an instrument therefore depends on its calibration, the charge and size ranges it samples, and its placement relative to the lander and its plasma wake [1].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a dust charging sensor. The examples below describe specific instruments and concepts from the sources accessed. Only the EDA sensor module has published mass and power values in those sources. The examples are not directly comparable: the EDA is a flight-qualified prototype with a defined measurement range, whereas the other concepts are breadboards, validation experiments or designs.

examples.name: Electrostatic Dust Analyzer (EDA), NASA DALI programme
examples.type: Flight-qualified prototype at TRL 6; no flight or lunar deployment reported in the sources accessed
examples.dimensions: Not given in the sources accessed.
examples.configuration: Two identical dust trajectory sensors, each with two arrays of seven wire electrodes (14 per sensor, 28 in total). Each wire is 8 cm long and 0.5 mm in diameter and has its own charge-sensitive amplifier. One deflection field electrode sits between the two sensors.
examples.field_of_view: 135 degrees for flux (first array only) and 54 degrees for size (all four arrays).
examples.design_ranges: Dust radius 1 to 20 micrometres; velocity 0.8 to 20 m/s; charge 1.2 to 64 fC; flux 0 to 1.7 particles per cm2 per s. Measurement requirements: radius 2 to 20 micrometres, velocity 1.25 to 10 m/s, charge 2.4 to 24 fC, flux 5e-5 to 0.5 particles per cm2 per s.
examples.laboratory_results: Vacuum chamber at 7e-7 Torr with JSC-1A simulant. Velocity within 4% and charge within 15% of estimates for 100 to 112 micrometre and 35 to 48 micrometre grains; a 4.6 fC charge resolved above a 0.5 fC noise floor. With a 1500 V deflection bias, size within 6% of the lower limit of the size distribution and velocity within 2%.
examples.environmental_qualification: GSFC-STD-7000 GEVS: vibration 14.1 grms in three axes at proto-flight level; quasi-static 42 g in three axes; thermal-vacuum survival cycle -50 to +85 C and four operational cycles -35 to +80 C.
examples.placement_guidance: Simulations suggest the sensor module should sit at least 1 m from the lander and outside its plasma wake.
examples.limitations: The digital signal processing module was out of scope and was replaced by a desktop computer in the prototype.

examples.name: Lunar Levitation Dust Instrument (DLR, Germany)
examples.type: Proposed lander concept with initial experimental validation; conference-stage, not peer-reviewed
examples.detection_method: 532 nm pulsed laser and a stereo camera system detect and characterise levitated dust within up to 10 m.
examples.modelling: Maximum height and exit velocity calculated for 1 to 10 micrometre particles; only under fast solar wind do particles gain enough electrostatic potential to escape the sheath.
examples.mass_power_dimensions_accuracy: Not stated in the source abstract.
examples.flight_status: No mission, launch or manifest named.

examples.name: DUSTER dust probe (European project)
examples.type: Breadboard instrument; project objectives reported as met
examples.components: Dust collector probe biased between -5000 V and +5000 V with current from charged particles measured in a Faraday cup; Langmuir probe for electron temperature, electron density and ion density; electric-field probe for the DC field just above the surface.
examples.technology_readiness_level: Not stated on the fetched project news page. A search summary cited TRL 4, which was not confirmed in a primary source.
examples.flight_status: Proposed as a candidate for ESA's AstroLEAP payload; no launch date given.

examples.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Ejecta and Meteorites (LEAM)
examples.type: Flown lunar surface experiment; data interpreted as charged-dust events
examples.deployment: Placed by the Apollo 17 crew in the Taurus-Littrow region. Source [5] gives December 1973; the Apollo 17 mission flew in December 1972. This article uses December 1972 and flags the conflict.
examples.measurement_basis: Analysis of impact data covering more than 22 lunations, with events concentrated during terminator passages.
examples.mechanism_proposed: Charged lunar fines held by adhesive forces can be ejected when electrostatic stress exceeds adhesive strength; a simple laboratory test was said to support transport at and near the terminator.
examples.instrument_design: Not verified in the sources accessed. Neither abstract quantifies the charge, the stress or the ejection rates.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The EDA sensor module dimensions are not given in the sources accessed. The EDA wire electrodes are 8 cm long and 0.5 mm in diameter. No dimensions are published in the sources accessed for the other examples. Dimensions and mounting interfaces would need to be determined from any future instrument's measurement geometry and mounting requirements.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The EDA sensor module has a mass of 4.3 kg. No mass is published in the sources accessed for the DLR concept, the DUSTER probe or LEAM.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The EDA sensor module power is 5 W. Power is not publicly specified in the sources accessed for the other examples.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A dust charging sensor on the surface would operate in vacuum, with extreme thermal cycling and a plasma and ultraviolet environment that drives dust charging [1][3]. The EDA's qualification tests cover vibration, quasi-static loads and thermal-vacuum cycling from -50 C to +85 C in survival and -35 C to +80 C in operation [1]. The paper's simulations also indicate that the sensor should sit at least 1 m from the lander and outside its plasma wake [1]. Dust deposition on sensing surfaces and electrostatic interaction between dust and hardware are the phenomena these instruments are meant to characterise [2]. The sources accessed do not quantify the effect of the lander's own charge on the measurements.
article.limitations: Charge is not size. EDA size depends on an assumed grain density of about 2.9 or 3 g cm-3 and carries that assumption [1]. The EDA design ranges limit the grain radii (1 to 20 micrometres), charges (1.2 to 64 fC) and flux (up to 1.7 particles per cm2 per s) it can report [1]; grains outside these ranges are not measured. The EDA is reported as flight-qualified, not flight-proven [1]. Mass, power, size and accuracy are not stated for the DLR concept [3] or the DUSTER probe [6]. The DUSTER project page gives no technology readiness level [6]; a search summary cited a level of 4, which was not confirmed in a primary source. The LEAM interpretation rests on abstracts, which do not quantify the charge or stress, so the electrostatic-stress-versus-adhesion argument cannot be checked here [5].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A dust charging sensor could be carried as a lander or rover payload, or as part of a surface experiment package. The sources accessed describe lander-type deployment only. No orbiter pathway is described, and no compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted.
transportation_process: Integrate the sensor into a lander or rover payload compartment on Earth.
Launch it into space using a launch vehicle.
Land it on the surface using a lander.
Deploy and position the sensor, keeping the EDA sensor module at least 1 m from the lander and outside its plasma wake [1].
Connect power and data, and level and thermally protect the sensor as required.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment method, mounting and interfaces for the DLR and DUSTER concepts are not verified in the sources accessed. The EDA placement guidance (at least 1 m from the lander, outside its plasma wake) is the only verified deployment constraint in the sources accessed [1].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 17 LEAM experiment was deployed by the crew as part of the Apollo lunar surface experiment programme [4][5].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: The EDA sensor module mass (4.3 kg) and power (5 W) are the only verified values relevant to transportation integration [1]. Dimensions and mounting interfaces are not published in the sources accessed. Compatibility with any lander would need verified mass, power, mounting, interface and placement data before it could be assessed.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 17 LEAM experiment is the earliest flown instrument in the sources accessed that recorded electrostatically charged lunar dust, although it was designed to measure cosmic-dust impacts [4][5]. Surveyor 6 had earlier recorded the horizon glow that is now associated with dust levitation [3]. The EDA, DUSTER and DLR concepts are more recent instruments designed specifically to measure or detect charged dust [1][3][6]. The ICES 2022 paper describes ground-stage instrumentation for measuring dust charge on space-rated materials [2].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: This article rests on abstracts, project pages and summarised fetches rather than full texts for most sources. The EDA figures were taken from the 2024 Planetary Science Journal article as read through a summarising fetch, and they should be checked line by line against the paper before use [1]. The 1976 and 1977 LEAM papers were accessible only as abstracts, so the instrument design, measurement values and dawn behaviour of the impact rate are not verified here [4][5]. The ICES 2022 paper's full text could not be read, so its instrument names, technology readiness and specifications are unknown [2]. The DUSTER technology readiness level is not stated [6], and the DLR abstract gives no test results [3]. No instrument under the exact name 'dust charging sensor' was identified, so the entry is treated as a measurement function. Assigning it to individual instruments is a decision for the catalogue owner, and catalogue entry 133 is the closest name match for the EDA. No verified image was found in this run, so no pictures are shown.

data_quality_notes: No instrument under the exact name 'dust charging sensor' was identified in the sources accessed. The article treats the entry as a measurement function covering several instruments and concepts; assignment to instruments is for the catalogue owner to decide. Catalogue entry 133 (Electrostatic dust analyser) is the closest name match for the EDA.
EDA figures (Table 1 values, mass, power, test results) were extracted through a summarising fetch of the 2024 Planetary Science Journal article and must be checked against the full paper.
The DUSTER technology readiness level is not stated on the fetched project news page. A search summary cited TRL 4, which was not confirmed.
Reference 5 gives the LEAM deployment as December 1973; the Apollo 17 mission flew in December 1972. The article uses December 1972 and flags the conflict.
Author order for reference 5 differs between two repository records; the order given follows the JAXA AIREX record.
Full texts of references 2, 4 and 5 could not be read. The PDF downloads returned compressed binary data, so the content comes from NTRS and JAXA metadata pages and abstracts.
Search summaries describing LEAM sensor axes and a dawn impact-rate increase were not confirmed against primary text and are not used.
No verified image asset was found; all image arrays are empty.
